l: Poland
Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a country in <color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color>. It extends from the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color> in the north to

the Sudetes and <color=#3366CC>Carpathian Mountains</color> in the south, and borders <color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color> and <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> to the northeast; <color=#3366CC>Belarus</color> and

<color=#3366CC>Ukraine</color> to the east; <color=#3366CC>Slovakia</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Czech Republic</color> to the south; and <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> to the west. The territory has a varied
landscape, diverse ecosystems, and a <color=#3366CC>temperate climate</color>. Poland is composed of sixteen voivodeships and is the fifth
most populous member state of the European Union (EU), with over 38 million people, and the fifth largest EU country
by land area, covering 312696 km2. The capital and largest city is <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color>; other major cities include <color=#3366CC>Kraków</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wrocław</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Łódź</color>, <color=#3366CC>Poznań</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Gdańsk</color>.
Prehistoric human activity on Polish soil dates to the <color=#3366CC>Lower Paleolithic</color>, with continuous settlement since the end of the
<color=#3366CC>Last Glacial Period</color>. Culturally diverse throughout <color=#3366CC>late antiquity</color>, in the <color=#3366CC>early medieval period</color> the region became
inhabited by the <color=#3366CC>West Slavic</color> tribal Polans, who gave Poland its name. The process of establishing <color=#3366CC>statehood</color> coincided
with the conversion of a <color=#3366CC>pagan ruler of the Polans</color> to Christianity in 966 under the auspices of the <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Church</color>. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025, and in 1569 cemented its long-standing association with Lithuania,
thus forming the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color>. At the time, the Commonwealth was one of the great powers of
Europe, with an elective monarchy and a uniquely liberal political system, which adopted Europe's first modern
constitution in 1791.
With the passing of the prosperous Polish Golden Age, the country was <color=#3366CC>partitioned by neighbouring states</color> at the end of
the 18th century. At the end of <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> in 1918, Poland regained its independence with the founding of the Second
Polish Republic, which emerged <color=#3366CC>victorious</color> in various conflicts of the interbellum period. In September 1939, the

<color=#3366CC>invasion of Poland</color> by <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> and <color=#3366CC>the invasion</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> marked the beginning of <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, which
resulted in the Holocaust and millions of Polish casualties as well as extensive border and demographic changes.
Forced into the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Bloc</color> in the global <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, the Polish People's Republic was a signatory of the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color>.
Through the 1980 emergence and contributions of the <color=#3366CC>Solidarity movement</color>, which initiated the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Iron Curtain</color>,
the communist government was <color=#3366CC>dissolved</color> and Poland as the first of the <color=#3366CC>communist</color> countries re-established itself as a
<color=#3366CC>liberal democracy</color> in 1989, and held free elections.
Poland is a parliamentary republic with its <color=#3366CC>bicameral legislature</color> comprising the Sejm and the Senate. Considered a
middle power and a <color=#3366CC>regional power</color>, it is a <color=#3366CC>developed country</color> with a developed market and high-income economy. In
terms of nominal GDP, it is the 20th largest economy in the world and the sixth in the European Union, and fifth largest
by PPP-adjusted GDP in the EU. Poland has free university education and universal health care. It has 18 UNESCO
<color=#3366CC>World Heritage Sites</color>, over 100 Historic Monuments and 23 national parks. Poland is a founding member of the <color=#3366CC>United</color>

<color=#3366CC>Nations</color>, and a member of the <color=#3366CC>Council of Europe</color>, <color=#3366CC>World Trade Organization</color>, <color=#3366CC>OECD</color>, <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>, and <color=#3366CC>EU</color> (including the
<color=#3366CC>Schengen Area</color>).
Etymology
The native <color=#3366CC>Polish</color> name for Poland is Polska. It is believed that the name derives from the Polans, a <color=#3366CC>West Slavic</color> tribe
who inhabited the Warta River basin of present-day Greater Poland region (6th–8th century CE). The tribe's name
stems from the Proto-Slavic noun pole, meaning field, which itself originates from the <color=#3366CC>Proto-Indo-European</color> word
*pleh2- indicating flatland. The etymology alludes to the <color=#3366CC>topography</color> of the region and the flat landscape of Greater
Poland. During the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> form Polonia was widely used throughout Europe.
The country's alternative archaic name is Lechia and its root syllable remains in official use in several languages,

notably <color=#3366CC>Hungarian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lithuanian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>. The exonym possibly derives from either <color=#3366CC>Lech</color>, a legendary ruler of the
Lechites, or from the Lendians, a West Slavic tribe that dwelt on the south-easternmost edge of Lesser Poland. The
origin of the tribe's name lies in the Old Polish word lęda (plain). Initially, both names Lechia and Polonia were used
interchangeably when referring to Poland by chroniclers during the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>.
History
Prehistory and protohistory
The first <color=#3366CC>Stone Age</color> archaic humans and <color=#3366CC>Homo erectus</color> species settled what was to become Poland approximately
500,000 years ago, though the ensuing hostile climate prevented early humans from founding more permanent
encampments. The arrival of <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> and <color=#3366CC>anatomically modern humans</color> coincided with the climatic discontinuity
at the end of the <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial Period</color> (Northern Polish glaciation 10,000 BC), when Poland became habitable. <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color>
excavations indicated broad-ranging development in that era; the earliest evidence of European cheesemaking (5500
BC) was discovered in Polish Kuyavia, and the Bronocice pot is incised with the earliest known depiction of what may
be a wheeled vehicle (3400 BC).
The period spanning the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Early Iron Age</color> (1300 BC–500 BC) was marked by an increase in
population density, establishment of <color=#3366CC>palisaded</color> settlements (gords) and the expansion of Lusatian culture. A significant
archaeological find from the protohistory of Poland is a fortified settlement at Biskupin, attributed to the Lusatian culture
of the <color=#3366CC>Late Bronze Age</color> (mid-8th century BC).
Throughout <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color> (400 BC–500 AD), many distinct ancient populations inhabited the territory of present-day Poland,

notably <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Scythian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sarmatian</color>, Baltic and <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> tribes. Furthermore, archaeological findings confirmed
the presence of <color=#3366CC>Roman Legions</color> sent to protect the <color=#3366CC>amber trade</color>. The Polish tribes emerged following the <color=#3366CC>second wave</color>
<color=#3366CC>of the Migration Period</color> around the 6th century AD; they were <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> and may have included assimilated remnants of
peoples that earlier dwelled in the area. Beginning in the early 10th century, the Polans would come to dominate other
Lechitic tribes in the region, initially forming a tribal federation and later a centralised monarchical state.
Kingdom of Poland
Poland began to form into a recognisable unitary and territorial entity around the middle of the 10th century under the
<color=#3366CC>Piast dynasty</color>. In 966, the ruler of the Polans, <color=#3366CC>Mieszko I</color>, accepted Western Christianity under the auspices of the
<color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic Church</color> which was tantamount to the adoption of <color=#3366CC>Christianity by Poland</color>. In 968, a missionary <color=#3366CC>bishopric</color>
was established in <color=#3366CC>Poznań</color>. An incipit titled Dagome iudex first defined Poland's geographical boundaries with its capital
in Gniezno and affirmed that its monarchy was under the protection of the Apostolic See. The country's early origins
were described by Gallus Anonymus in Gesta principum Polonorum, the oldest Polish chronicle. An important national
event of the period was the <color=#3366CC>martyrdom</color> of Saint Adalbert, who was killed by <color=#3366CC>Prussian</color> pagans in 997 and whose remains
were reputedly bought back for their weight in gold by Mieszko's successor, <color=#3366CC>Bolesław I the Brave</color>.
In 1000, at the Congress of Gniezno, Bolesław I the Brave obtained the right of investiture from <color=#3366CC>Otto III, Holy Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Emperor</color>, who assented to the creation archdioceses in Gniezno and three new dioceses on Polish lands in <color=#3366CC>Kraków</color>,
Kołobrzeg, and <color=#3366CC>Wrocław</color>. Also, Otto bestowed upon Bolesław royal regalia and a replica of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Lance</color>, which were
later used at his coronation as the first King of Poland c. 1025, when Bolesław received permission for his coronation
from Pope John XIX. Bolesław also expanded the realm considerably by seizing parts of German Lusatia, Czech
<color=#3366CC>Moravia</color>, Upper Hungary, and southwestern regions of the <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus'</color>.
The transition from <color=#3366CC>paganism</color> in Poland was not instantaneous and resulted in the pagan reaction of the 1030s. In
1031, Mieszko II Lambert lost the title of king and fled amidst the violence. The unrest led to the transfer of the capital
to Kraków in 1038 by <color=#3366CC>Casimir I the Restorer</color>. In 1076, Bolesław II re-instituted the office of king, but was banished in
1079 for murdering his opponent, Bishop Stanislaus. In 1138, the country fragmented into five principalities when
<color=#3366CC>Bolesław III Wrymouth</color> divided his lands among his sons. These were Lesser Poland, Greater Poland, <color=#3366CC>Silesia</color>, Masovia,
and Sandomierz, with intermittent hold over <color=#3366CC>Pomerania</color>. In 1226, Konrad I of Masovia invited the <color=#3366CC>Teutonic Knights</color> to
aid in combating the Baltic Prussians; a decision that later led to centuries of warfare with the Knights.
In the first half of the 13th century, Henry I the Bearded and Henry II the Pious aimed to unite the fragmented
dukedoms, but the Mongol invasion and the death of Henry II in battle hindered the unification. As a result of the
devastation which followed, depopulation and the demand for craft labour spurred a migration of German and Flemish
settlers into Poland, which was encouraged by the Polish dukes. In 1264, the Statute of Kalisz introduced
unprecedented autonomy for the Polish Jews, who came to Poland fleeing persecution elsewhere in Europe.
In 1320, <color=#3366CC>Władysław I the Short</color> became the first king of a reunified Poland since Przemysł II in 1296, and the first to be
crowned at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. Beginning in 1333, the reign of <color=#3366CC>Casimir III the Great</color> was marked by
developments in castle infrastructure, army, judiciary and diplomacy. Under his authority, Poland transformed into a
major European power; he instituted Polish rule over <color=#3366CC>Ruthenia</color> in 1340 and imposed quarantine that prevented the
spread of <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>. In 1364, Casimir inaugurated the <color=#3366CC>University of Kraków</color>, one of the oldest institutions of higher
learning in Europe. Upon his death in 1370, the Piast dynasty came to an end. He was succeeded by his closest male

relative, <color=#3366CC>Louis of Anjou</color>, who ruled Poland, <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color> in a personal union. Louis' younger daughter <color=#3366CC>Jadwiga</color>
became Poland's first female monarch in 1384.
The Golden Age
In 1386, Jadwiga of Poland entered a marriage of convenience with <color=#3366CC>Władysław II Jagiełło</color>, the Grand Duke of Lithuania,
thus forming the <color=#3366CC>Jagiellonian dynasty</color> and the Polish–Lithuanian union which spanned the late <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> and early
<color=#3366CC>Modern Era</color>. The partnership between Poles and Lithuanians brought the vast multi-ethnic <color=#3366CC>Lithuanian</color> territories into
Poland's sphere of influence and proved beneficial for its inhabitants, who coexisted in one of the largest European
political entities of the time.
In the Baltic Sea region, the struggle of Poland and Lithuania with the <color=#3366CC>Teutonic Knights</color> continued and culminated at the
<color=#3366CC>Battle of Grunwald</color> in 1410, where a combined Polish–Lithuanian army inflicted a decisive victory against them. In
1466, after the Thirteen Years' War, king <color=#3366CC>Casimir IV Jagiellon</color> gave royal consent to the Peace of Thorn, which created
the future Duchy of Prussia under Polish suzerainty and forced the Prussian rulers to pay tributes. The Jagiellonian
dynasty also established dynastic control over the kingdoms of <color=#3366CC>Bohemia</color> (1471 onwards) and Hungary. In the south,
Poland confronted the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> (at the Varna Crusade) and the <color=#3366CC>Crimean Tatars</color>, and in the east helped
Lithuania to combat <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>.
Poland was developing as a <color=#3366CC>feudal</color> state, with a predominantly agricultural economy and an increasingly powerful
landed nobility that confined the population to private manorial farmstead known as folwarks. In 1493, John I Albert
sanctioned the creation of a <color=#3366CC>bicameral parliament</color> (the Sejm) composed of a lower house, the chamber of deputies, and
an upper house, the chamber of senators. The Nihil novi act adopted by the Polish General Sejm in 1505, transferred
most of the <color=#3366CC>legislative power</color> from the monarch to the parliament, an event which marked the beginning of the period
known as Golden Liberty, when the state was ruled by the seemingly free and equal Polish nobles.
The 16th century saw <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color> movements making deep inroads into Polish Christianity, which resulted
in the establishment of policies promoting religious tolerance, unique in Europe at that time. This tolerance allowed the
country to avoid the religious turmoil and <color=#3366CC>wars of religion</color> that beset Europe. In Poland, <color=#3366CC>Nontrinitarian Christianity</color>
became the doctrine of the so-called Polish Brethren, who separated from their <color=#3366CC>Calvinist</color> denomination and became the
co-founders of global <color=#3366CC>Unitarianism</color>.
The European <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> evoked under <color=#3366CC>Sigismund I the Old</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sigismund II Augustus</color> a sense of urgency in the
need to promote a cultural awakening. During the Polish Golden Age, the nation's economy and culture flourished. The
Italian-born Bona Sforza, daughter of the Duke of Milan and queen consort to Sigismund I, made considerable
contributions to architecture, <color=#3366CC>cuisine</color>, language and court customs at Wawel Castle.
Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
The <color=#3366CC>Union of Lublin</color> of 1569 established the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color>, a unified federal state with an <color=#3366CC>elective</color>
<color=#3366CC>monarchy</color> that was largely governed by the nobility. The latter coincided with a period of prosperity. The
Polish-dominated union thereafter became a leading power and a major cultural entity, exercising political control over
parts of Central, <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>, Southeastern and Northern Europe. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth occupied
approximately 1 e6km2 at its peak and was the largest state in Europe. Simultaneously, Poland imposed Polonisation
policies in newly acquired territories which were met with resistance from ethnic and religious minorities.
In 1573, <color=#3366CC>Henry de Valois of France</color>, the first elected king, approbated the Henrician Articles which obliged future
monarchs to respect the rights of nobles. When he left Poland to become King of France, his successor, <color=#3366CC>Stephen</color>
<color=#3366CC>Báthory</color>, led a successful campaign in the <color=#3366CC>Livonian War</color>, granting Poland more <color=#3366CC>lands across the eastern shores</color> of the
Baltic Sea. State affairs were then headed by Jan Zamoyski, the Crown Chancellor. Stephen's successor, <color=#3366CC>Sigismund</color>
<color=#3366CC>III</color>, defeated a rival <color=#3366CC>Habsburg</color> electoral candidate, Archduke Maximilian III, in the War of the Polish Succession
(1587–1588). In 1592, Sigismund succeeded his father John Vasa, in <color=#3366CC>Sweden</color>. The Polish-Swedish union endured until
1599, when he was deposed by the Swedes.
In 1609, Sigismund <color=#3366CC>invaded</color> <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> which was engulfed in a <color=#3366CC>civil war</color>, and a year later the Polish winged hussar units
under Stanisław Żółkiewski occupied Moscow for two years after defeating the Russians at Klushino. Sigismund also
countered the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> in the southeast; at Khotyn in 1621 <color=#3366CC>Jan Karol Chodkiewicz</color> achieved a decisive victory
against the Turks, which ushered the downfall of Sultan Osman II. Sigismund's long reign in Poland coincided with the
<color=#3366CC>Silver Age</color>. The liberal <color=#3366CC>Władysław IV</color> effectively defended Poland's territorial possessions but after his death the vast
Commonwealth began declining from internal disorder and constant warfare.
In 1648, the Polish hegemony over Ukraine sparked the Khmelnytsky Uprising, followed by the decimating Swedish
Deluge during the <color=#3366CC>Second Northern War</color>, and Prussia's independence in 1657. In 1683, <color=#3366CC>John III Sobieski</color> re-established
military prowess when he halted the advance of an Ottoman Army into Europe at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Vienna</color>. The Saxon era,
under <color=#3366CC>Augustus II</color> and <color=#3366CC>Augustus III</color>, saw neighbouring powers grow in strength at the expense of Poland. Both Saxon
kings faced opposition from <color=#3366CC>Stanisław Leszczyński</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Great Northern War</color> (1700) and the War of the Polish
Succession (1733).
Partitions
The royal election of 1764 resulted in the elevation of <color=#3366CC>Stanisław II Augustus Poniatowski</color> to the monarchy. His
candidacy was extensively funded by his sponsor and former lover, Empress <color=#3366CC>Catherine II of Russia</color>. The new king
maneuvered between his desire to implement necessary modernising reforms, and the necessity to remain at peace
with surrounding states. His ideals led to the formation of the 1768 Bar Confederation, a rebellion directed against the
Poniatowski and all external influence, which ineptly aimed to preserve Poland's sovereignty and privileges held by the
nobility. The failed attempts at government restructuring as well as the domestic turmoil provoked its neighbours to
invade.
In 1772, the First Partition of the Commonwealth by Prussia, Russia, and Austria took place, an act which the Partition
Sejm, under considerable duress, eventually ratified as a fait accompli. Disregarding the territorial losses, in 1773 a
plan of critical reforms was established, in which the Commission of National Education, the first government education
authority in Europe, was inaugurated. Corporal punishment of schoolchildren was officially prohibited in 1783.
Poniatowski was the head figure of the Enlightenment, encouraged the development of industries, and embraced
republican <color=#3366CC>neoclassicism</color>. For his contributions to the arts and sciences, he was awarded a Fellowship of the Royal
Society.
In 1791, the Great Sejm parliament adopted the 3 May Constitution, the first set of supreme national laws, and
introduced a <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color>. The Targowica Confederation, an organisation of nobles and deputies opposing
the act, appealed to Catherine and caused the 1792 Polish–Russian War. Fearing the reemergence of Polish
hegemony, Russia and Prussia arranged and, in 1793, executed the Second Partition, which left the country deprived
of territory and incapable of independent existence. On 24 October 1795, the Commonwealth was partitioned for the
third time and ceased to exist as a territorial entity. Stanisław Augustus, the last King of Poland, abdicated the throne
on 25 November 1795.
Era of insurrections
The Polish people rose several times against the partitioners and occupying armies. An unsuccessful attempt at
defending Poland's sovereignty took place in the 1794 <color=#3366CC>Kościuszko Uprising</color>, where a popular and distinguished general
<color=#3366CC>Tadeusz Kościuszko</color>, who had several years earlier served under <color=#3366CC>George Washington</color> in the <color=#3366CC>American Revolutionary</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color>, led Polish insurgents. Despite the victory at the Battle of Racławice, his ultimate defeat ended Poland's
independent existence for 123 years.
In 1806, an insurrection organised by Jan Henryk Dąbrowski liberated western Poland ahead of <color=#3366CC>Napoleon</color>'s advance
into Prussia during the <color=#3366CC>War of the Fourth Coalition</color>. In accordance with the 1807 Treaty of Tilsit, Napoleon proclaimed
the Duchy of Warsaw, a client state ruled by his ally Frederick Augustus I of Saxony. The Poles actively aided French
troops in the <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color>, particularly those under Józef Poniatowski who became Marshal of France shortly
before his death at <color=#3366CC>Leipzig</color> in 1813. In the aftermath of Napoleon's exile, the Duchy of Warsaw was abolished at the
<color=#3366CC>Congress of Vienna</color> in 1815 and its territory was divided into Russian Congress Kingdom of Poland, the Prussian
Grand Duchy of Posen, and Austrian Galicia with the Free City of Kraków.
In 1830, <color=#3366CC>non-commissioned officers</color> at Warsaw's Officer Cadet School rebelled in what was the November Uprising.
After its collapse, Congress Poland lost its constitutional autonomy, army and legislative assembly. During the
<color=#3366CC>European Spring of Nations</color>, Poles took up arms in the Greater Poland Uprising of 1848 to resist Germanisation, but its
failure saw the duchy's status reduced to a mere province; and subsequent integration into the <color=#3366CC>German Empire</color> in 1871.
In Russia, the fall of the January Uprising (1863–1864) prompted severe political, social and cultural reprisals, followed
by deportations and <color=#3366CC>pogroms</color> of the Polish-Jewish population. Towards the end of the 19th century, Congress Poland
became heavily industrialised; its primary exports being coal, <color=#3366CC>zinc</color>, iron and textiles.
Second Polish Republic
In the aftermath of <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color> agreed on the reconstitution of Poland, confirmed through the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Versailles</color> of June 1919. A total of 2 million Poles served in the armies of the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the
Russian Empire, and over 450,000 died. Following the armistice with Germany in November 1918, Poland regained its
independence as the Second Polish Republic.
The Second Polish Republic reaffirmed its sovereignty after a series of military conflicts, most notably the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Soviet</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color>, when Poland inflicted a crushing defeat on the <color=#3366CC>Red Army</color> at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Warsaw</color>.
The inter-war period heralded a new era of Polish politics. Whilst Polish political activists had faced heavy censorship in
the decades up until <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, a new political tradition was established in the country. Many exiled Polish activists,
such as <color=#3366CC>Ignacy Jan Paderewski</color>, who would later become prime minister, returned home. A significant number of them
then went on to take key positions in the newly formed political and governmental structures. Tragedy struck in 1922
when Gabriel Narutowicz, inaugural holder of the presidency, was assassinated at the Zachęta Gallery in Warsaw by a
painter and right-wing nationalist Eligiusz Niewiadomski.
In 1926, the May Coup, led by the hero of the Polish independence campaign Marshal <color=#3366CC>Józef Piłsudski</color>, turned rule of
the Second Polish Republic over to the nonpartisan Sanacja (Healing) movement to prevent radical political
organisations on both the left and the right from destabilising the country. By the late 1930s, due to increased threats
posed by political extremism inside the country, the Polish government became increasingly heavy-handed, banning a
number of radical organisations, including communist and ultra-nationalist political parties, which threatened the
stability of the country.
World War II
World War II began with the <color=#3366CC>Nazi German</color> <color=#3366CC>invasion of Poland</color> on 1 September 1939, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Soviet invasion of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Poland</color> on 17 September. As agreed in the <color=#3366CC>Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact</color>, Poland was split into two zones, one occupied by
Nazi Germany, the other by the Soviet Union. The wartime resistance movement, and the <color=#3366CC>Armia Krajowa</color> (Home Army),
fought against the occupation. It was one of the three largest resistance movements of the entire war, and
encompassed a range of clandestine activities, which functioned as an underground state complete with
degree-awarding universities and a court system. The resistance was loyal to the Polish Government in Exile and
generally resented the idea of a post-war communist Poland; for this reason, in the summer of 1944 it initiated
Operation Tempest, of which the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Uprising</color> that began on 1 August 1944 is the best-known operation.
Poland made the fourth-largest troop contribution in Europe, and its troops served both the exiled government in the
west and Soviet leadership in the east. Polish troops played an important role in the Normandy, <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>, <color=#3366CC>North African</color>
<color=#3366CC>Campaigns</color> and Netherlands and are particularly remembered for the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Britain</color> and Battle of Monte Cassino.
Polish intelligence operatives proved extremely valuable to the Allies, providing much of the intelligence from Europe
and beyond, Polish code breakers were responsible for cracking the Enigma cipher and Polish scientists participating in
the <color=#3366CC>Manhattan Project</color> were co-creators of the American <color=#3366CC>atomic bomb</color>. In the east, the Soviet-backed Polish 1st Army
distinguished itself in the battles for <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color> and <color=#3366CC>Berlin</color>.
The actions undertaken by both occupiers within Polish territory were <color=#3366CC>genocidal</color>. In 1939–1941, the Soviets deported
hundreds of thousands of Poles and the Soviet NKVD executed thousands of Polish <color=#3366CC>prisoners of war</color> ahead of
<color=#3366CC>Operation Barbarossa</color>, notably in the <color=#3366CC>Katyn massacre</color>. Around 150,000 Polish civilians were killed by Soviets during the
Soviet Union's occupation of eastern Poland (<color=#3366CC>Kresy</color>). Similarly, German planners had in November 1939 called for "the
complete destruction of all Poles" and their fate as outlined in the <color=#3366CC>Generalplan Ost</color>; six German <color=#3366CC>extermination camps</color>
were established in occupied Poland, including Treblinka, Majdanek and <color=#3366CC>Auschwitz</color>. The Germans <color=#3366CC>transported millions</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Jews</color> from across occupied Europe to be murdered in those camps. Altogether, 3 million Polish Jews –
approximately 90% of Poland's pre-war Jewry – and between 1.8 and 2.8 million ethnic Poles were killed, including up
to 100,000 members of the Polish intelligentsia. The <color=#3366CC>Romani people</color> were also exterminated. During the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color>
<color=#3366CC>Uprising</color> alone, over 150,000 Polish civilians were killed, most were murdered by the Germans during the Wola and
Ochota massacres. At least 100,000 Poles were also murdered by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) between 1943
and 1944 in what became known as the Wołyń Massacres.
<color=#3366CC>Of all the countries</color> in the war, Poland lost the highest percentage of its citizens: around 6 million perished – more than
one-sixth of Poland's pre-war population – half of them Polish Jews. About 90% of deaths were non-military in nature.
In 1945, Poland's borders were shifted westwards. The shift forced the migration of millions of people. Over two million
Polish inhabitants of <color=#3366CC>Kresy</color> <color=#3366CC>were expelled</color> along the Curzon Line by <color=#3366CC>Stalin</color>. Up to eight million Germans were expelled
by Poland from the territories it acquired. The western border became the <color=#3366CC>Oder-Neisse line</color>. As a result, Poland's
territory was reduced by 20%, or 77500 km2.
Post-war communism
At the insistence of <color=#3366CC>Joseph Stalin</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Yalta Conference</color> sanctioned the formation of a new provisional pro-Communist
coalition government in Moscow, which ignored the Polish government-in-exile based in London. This action angered
many Poles who considered it a betrayal by the Allies. In 1944, Stalin had made guarantees to <color=#3366CC>Churchill</color> and <color=#3366CC>Roosevelt</color>
that he would maintain Poland's sovereignty and allow democratic elections to take place. However, upon achieving
victory in 1945, the elections organised by the occupying Soviet authorities were falsified and were used to provide a
veneer of legitimacy for Soviet hegemony over Polish affairs. The Soviet Union instituted a new communist government
in Poland, analogous to much of the rest of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Bloc</color>. As elsewhere in Communist Europe, the Soviet influence
over Poland was met with armed resistance from the outset which continued into the 1950s.
Despite widespread objections, the new Polish government accepted the Soviet annexation of the pre-war eastern
regions of Poland (in particular the cities of <color=#3366CC>Wilno</color> and <color=#3366CC>Lwów</color>) and agreed to the permanent garrisoning of <color=#3366CC>Red Army</color>
units on Poland's territory. Military alignment within the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> throughout the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> came about as a direct
result of this change in Poland's political culture. In the European scene, it came to characterise the full-fledged
integration of Poland into the brotherhood of communist nations.
The new communist government took control with the adoption of the Small Constitution on 19 February 1947. The
Polish People's Republic (Polska Rzeczpospolita Ludowa) was officially proclaimed in 1952. In 1956, after the death of
<color=#3366CC>Bolesław Bierut</color>, the régime of <color=#3366CC>Władysław Gomułka</color> became temporarily more liberal, freeing many people from prison
and expanding some personal freedoms. Collectivisation in the Polish People's Republic failed. A similar situation
repeated itself in the 1970s under <color=#3366CC>Edward Gierek</color>, but most of the time persecution of anti-communist opposition
groups persisted. Despite this, Poland was at the time considered to be one of the least oppressive states of the
Eastern Bloc.
Labour turmoil in 1980 led to the formation of the independent trade union "<color=#3366CC>Solidarity</color>" ("Solidarność"), which over time
became a political force. Despite persecution and imposition of martial law in 1981 by General <color=#3366CC>Wojciech Jaruzelski</color>, it
eroded the dominance of the Polish United Workers' Party and by 1989 had triumphed in Poland's first partially free and
democratic parliamentary elections since the end of the Second World War. <color=#3366CC>Lech Wałęsa</color>, a Solidarity candidate,
eventually won the presidency in 1990. The Solidarity movement heralded the <color=#3366CC>collapse of communist regimes and</color>
<color=#3366CC>parties across Europe</color>.
Third Polish Republic
A shock therapy programme, initiated by Leszek Balcerowicz in the early 1990s, enabled the country to transform its
Soviet-style <color=#3366CC>planned economy</color> into a <color=#3366CC>market economy</color>. As with other post-communist countries, Poland suffered
temporary declines in social, economic, and living standards, but it became the first post-communist country to reach its
pre-1989 <color=#3366CC>GDP levels</color> as early as 1995, although the unemployment rate increased. Poland became a member of the
<color=#3366CC>Visegrád Group</color> in 1991, and joined <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> in 1999. Poles then voted to join the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> in a referendum in
June 2003, with Poland becoming a full member on 1 May 2004, following the consequent enlargement of the union.
Poland joined the <color=#3366CC>Schengen Area</color> in 2007, as a result of which, the country's borders with other member states of the
<color=#3366CC>European Union</color> were dismantled, allowing for <color=#3366CC>full freedom of movement</color> within most of the European Union. On 10
April 2010, the President of Poland <color=#3366CC>Lech Kaczyński</color>, along with 89 other high-ranking Polish officials died in a plane
crash near Smolensk, Russia.
In 2011, the ruling Civic Platform won parliamentary elections. In 2014, the Prime Minister of Poland, <color=#3366CC>Donald Tusk</color>, was
chosen to be President of the European Council, and resigned as prime minister. The 2015 and 2019 elections were
won by the national-conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) led by Jarosław Kaczyński, resulting in increased
Euroscepticism and increased friction with the European Union. In December 2017, Mateusz Morawiecki was sworn in
as the Prime Minister, succeeding Beata Szydlo, in office since 2015. President Andrzej Duda, supported by Law and
Justice party, was re-elected in the 2020 presidential election.
As of November 2023, the <color=#3366CC>Russian invasion of Ukraine</color> had led to 17 million Ukrainian refugees crossing the border to
Poland. As of November 2023, 0.9 million of those had stayed in Poland. In October 2023, the ruling Law and Justice
(PiS) party won the largest share of the vote in the election, but lost its majority in parliament. In December 2023,
Donald Tusk became the new Prime Minister leading a coalition made up of Civic Coalition, Third Way, and The Left.
Law and Justice became the leading opposition party.
On 1 June 2025, The Law and Justice candidate for the 2025 Polish presidential election, Karol Nawrocki won the
election, beating Civic Platform candidate Rafał Trzaskowski. The results continued the streak of Law and Justice
aligned presidential candidates only losing one presidential election in 2010 since its founding in 2001.
Geography
Poland covers an administrative area of 312722 km2, and is the ninth-largest country in Europe. Approximately 311895
km2 of the country's territory consists of land, 2041 km2 is internal waters and 8783 km2 is territorial sea.
Topographically, the landscape of Poland is characterised by diverse <color=#3366CC>landforms</color>, <color=#3366CC>water bodies</color> and <color=#3366CC>ecosystems</color>. The
central and northern region bordering the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color> lie within the flat <color=#3366CC>Central European Plain</color>, but its south is hilly and
mountainous. The average <color=#3366CC>elevation above the sea level</color> is estimated at 173 metres.
The country has a coastline spanning 770 km; extending from the shores of the Baltic Sea, along the Bay of Pomerania
in the west to the Gulf of Gdańsk in the east. The beach coastline is abundant in <color=#3366CC>sand dune fields</color> or coastal ridges and
is indented by spits and lagoons, notably the Hel Peninsula and the Vistula Lagoon, which is shared with Russia. The
largest Polish island on the Baltic Sea is Wolin, located within Wolin National Park. Poland also shares the Szczecin
Lagoon and the Usedom island with Germany.
The mountainous belt in the extreme south of Poland is divided into two major <color=#3366CC>mountain ranges</color>; the Sudetes in the
west and the <color=#3366CC>Carpathians</color> in the east. The highest part of the Carpathian massif are the Tatra Mountains, extending
along Poland's southern border. Poland's highest point is the northwestern summit of Rysy at 2500 m in elevation,
located in the Tatras. The highest summit of the Sudetes massif is Mount Śnieżka at 1603.3 m, shared with the Czech
Republic. The lowest point in Poland situated at Marzęcino on the Vistula Fens, which is 2.2 m below sea level.
In Poland, Trójmorski Wierch is one of the six tripoints of the European watershed.
Poland's longest rivers are the <color=#3366CC>Vistula</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Oder</color>, the Warta, and the Bug. The country also possesses one of the
highest densities of lakes in the world, numbering around ten thousand and mostly concentrated in the north-eastern
region of Masuria, within the Masurian Lake District. The largest lakes, covering more than 100 km2, are Śniardwy and
Mamry, and the deepest is Lake Hańcza at 108.5 m in depth.
Climate
The climate of Poland is <color=#3366CC>temperate transitional</color>, and varies from oceanic in the north-west to <color=#3366CC>continental</color> in the
south-east. The mountainous southern fringes are situated within an <color=#3366CC>alpine climate</color>. Poland is characterised by warm
summers, with a mean temperature of around 20 °C in July, and moderately cold winters averaging -1.2 °C in January.
In summer, maximum temperatures can reach 40 °C, while in winter in the Tatra Mountains and Bieszczady Mountains
they can even drop below -30 °C.
The warmest and sunniest part of Poland is Lower Silesia in the southwest and the coldest region is the northeast
corner, around Suwałki and Olecko where the climate is affected by cold fronts from <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Precipitation</color> is more frequent during the summer months, with highest rainfall recorded from June to September.
There is a considerable fluctuation in day-to-day weather and the arrival of a particular season can differ each year.
<color=#3366CC>Climate change</color> and other factors have further contributed to interannual thermal anomalies and increased
temperatures; the average annual air temperature between 2011 and 2020 was 9.33 °C, around 1.11 °C higher than in
the 2001–2010 period. Winters are also becoming increasingly drier, with less <color=#3366CC>snowfall</color>.
Biodiversity
Phytogeographically, Poland belongs to the Central European province of the Circumboreal Region within the Boreal
Kingdom. The country has four Palearctic ecoregions – Central, Northern, Western European <color=#3366CC>temperate broadleaf and</color>
<color=#3366CC>mixed forest</color>, and the Carpathian montane conifer. Forests occupy 31% of Poland's land area, the largest of which is
the Lower Silesian Wilderness. The most common deciduous trees found across the country are <color=#3366CC>oak</color>, <color=#3366CC>maple</color>, and

<color=#3366CC>beech</color>; the most common conifers are <color=#3366CC>pine</color>, <color=#3366CC>spruce</color>, and <color=#3366CC>fir</color>. An estimated 69% of all forests are <color=#3366CC>coniferous</color>.
The flora and fauna in Poland is that of <color=#3366CC>Continental Europe</color>, with the <color=#3366CC>wisent</color>, <color=#3366CC>white stork</color> and white-tailed eagle
designated as national animals, and the red common poppy being the unofficial floral emblem. Among the most
protected species is the <color=#3366CC>European bison</color>, Europe's heaviest land animal, as well as the Eurasian beaver, the northern
lynx, the Eurasian wolf and the Tatra chamois. The region was also home to the extinct <color=#3366CC>aurochs</color>, the last individual
dying in Poland in 1627. Game animals such as red deer, <color=#3366CC>roe deer</color>, and wild boar are found in most woodlands. Poland
is also a significant breeding ground for <color=#3366CC>migratory birds</color> and hosts around one quarter of the global population of white
storks.
Around 315100 ha, equivalent to 1% of Poland's territory, is protected within 23 Polish national parks, two of which –
<color=#3366CC>Białowieża</color> and Bieszczady – are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. There are 123 areas designated as landscape parks,
along with numerous <color=#3366CC>nature reserves</color> and other protected areas under the Natura 2000 network.
Government and politics
Poland is a <color=#3366CC>unitary</color> parliamentary republic and a <color=#3366CC>representative democracy</color>, with a president as the <color=#3366CC>head of state</color>. The
executive power is exercised further by the Council of Ministers and the prime minister who acts as the <color=#3366CC>head of</color>
<color=#3366CC>government</color>. The council's individual members are selected by the prime minister, approved by parliament and sworn in
by the president. The head of state is elected by popular vote for a five-year term. The current president is Karol
Nawrocki and the prime minister is <color=#3366CC>Donald Tusk</color>.
Poland's <color=#3366CC>legislative</color> assembly is a <color=#3366CC>bicameral</color> parliament consisting of a 460-member lower house (Sejm) and a
100-member upper house (Senate). The Sejm is elected under proportional representation according to the d'Hondt
method for vote–seat conversion. The Senate is elected under the first-past-the-post electoral system, with one senator
being returned from each of the one hundred constituencies. The Senate has the right to amend or reject a statute
passed by the Sejm, but the Sejm may override the Senate's decision with a majority vote.
With the exception of ethnic minority parties, only candidates of political parties receiving at least 5% of the total
national vote can enter the Sejm. Both the lower and upper houses of parliament in Poland are elected for a four-year
term and each member of the Polish parliament is guaranteed parliamentary immunity. Under current legislation, a
person must be 21 years of age or over to assume the position of deputy, 30 or over to become senator and 35 to run
in a presidential election.
Members of the Sejm and Senate jointly form the National Assembly of the Republic of Poland. The National Assembly,
headed by the marshal of the Sejm, or marshal of the Senate in their absence, is formed on three occasions – when a
new president takes the <color=#3366CC>oath of office</color>; when an indictment against the president is brought to the State Tribunal; and
for a declaration of the president's permanent incapacity to exercise his duties due to the state of his health.
According to International IDEA's Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices and Democracy Tracker, Poland performs
in the mid-range on overall democratic measures, with particular weaknesses in civic engagement and judicial
independence.
Administrative divisions
Poland is divided into 16 provinces or states known as voivodeships. As of 2022, the voivodeships are subdivided into
380 counties (powiats), which are further fragmented into 2,477 municipalities (gminas). Major cities normally have the
status of both gmina and powiat. The provinces are largely founded on the borders of historic regions, or named for
individual cities. Administrative authority at the voivodeship level is shared between a government-appointed governor
(voivode), an elected regional assembly (sejmik) and a voivodeship marshal, an executive elected by the assembly.
Law
The Constitution of Poland is the enacted supreme law, and Polish judicature is based on the principle of civil rights,
governed by the code of <color=#3366CC>civil law</color>. The current democratic constitution was adopted by the National Assembly of Poland
on 2 April 1997; it guarantees a multi-party state with freedoms of religion, speech and gatherings, prohibits the
practices of forced <color=#3366CC>medical experimentation</color>, torture or <color=#3366CC>corporal punishment</color>, and acknowledges the inviolability of the
home, the right to form trade unions, and the right to <color=#3366CC>strike</color>.
The judiciary in Poland is composed of the Supreme Court as the country's highest judicial organ, the Supreme
Administrative Court for the judicial control of public administration, Common Courts (District, Regional, Appellate) and
the <color=#3366CC>Military Court</color>. The Constitutional and State Tribunals are separate judicial bodies, which rule the constitutional
liability of people holding the highest offices of state and supervise the compliance of <color=#3366CC>statutory law</color>, thus protecting the
Constitution. Judges are nominated by the National Council of the Judiciary and are appointed for life by the president.
With the approval of the Senate, the Sejm appoints an <color=#3366CC>ombudsman</color> for a five-year term to guard the observance of
social justice.
Poland has a low <color=#3366CC>homicide</color> rate at 0.7 murders per 100,000 people, as of 2018. Rape, assault and violent crime remain
at a very low level. The country has imposed strict regulations on abortion, which is permitted only in cases of <color=#3366CC>rape</color>,
<color=#3366CC>incest</color> or when the woman's life is in danger; <color=#3366CC>congenital disorder</color> is not covered by the law, prompting some women to
seek abortion abroad.
Historically, the most significant Polish legal act is the Constitution of 3 May 1791. Instituted to redress long-standing
political defects of the <color=#3366CC>federative</color> <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color> and its Golden Liberty, it was the first modern
constitution in Europe and influenced many later <color=#3366CC>democratic movements</color> across the globe. In 1918, the Second Polish
Republic became one of the first countries to introduce universal <color=#3366CC>women's suffrage</color>.
Foreign relations
Poland is a middle power and a <color=#3366CC>regional power</color> in Europe. It has a total of 53 representatives in the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>Parliament</color> as of 2024. <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color> serves as the headquarters for Frontex, the European Union's agency for external
border security as well as ODIHR, one of the principal institutions of the <color=#3366CC>OSCE</color>. Apart from the European Union, Poland
has been a member of <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>, the United Nations, the <color=#3366CC>World Trade Organization</color> and regional alliances such as the
<color=#3366CC>Visegrád Group</color>, the Weimar Triangle and the Polish-led Three Seas Initiative.
In recent years, Poland significantly strengthened its relations with the United States, becoming one of its closest allies
and strategic partners in Europe. Historically, Poland maintained strong cultural and political ties with Hungary and
France.
Military
The Polish Armed Forces are composed of five branches – the Land Forces, the Navy, the Air Force, the Special
Forces and the Territorial Defence Force. The military is subordinate to the Ministry of National Defence of the Republic
of Poland. However, its commander-in-chief in peacetime is the president, who nominates officers, the Minister for
National Defence and the chief of staff. Polish military tradition is generally commemorated by the Armed Forces Day,
celebrated annually on 15 August. In July 2024, the Polish Armed Forces had a combined strength of 216,100 active
soldiers, making it the largest standing army in the European Union and the third largest in <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>.
Poland ranks 14th in the world in terms of military expenditures; the country allocated 4.12% of its total GDP on military
spending, equivalent to approximately US$35 billion in 2024. From 2022, Poland initiated a programme of mass
modernisation of its armed forces, in close cooperation with American, South Korean and local Polish defence
manufacturers concentrated in the Polish Armaments Group. Also, the Polish military is set to increase its size to
250,000 enlisted and officers, and 50,000 Territorial Defence Force. According to SIPRI, the country exported €487
million worth of arms and armaments to foreign countries in 2020.
Compulsory <color=#3366CC>military service</color> for men, was discontinued in 2008. Polish military doctrine reflects the same defensive
nature as that of its NATO partners and the country actively hosts NATO's <color=#3366CC>military exercises</color>. The Polish Special
Forces, consisting of six units (Grom, Formoza, Agat, Nil, Commandos Military Unit), have the authority to command
full-scale as well as joint NATO operations, with special forces from all NATO member states. Since 1953, the country
has been a large contributor to various United Nations peacekeeping missions, and currently maintains military
presence in the Middle East, Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Baltic states</color> and southeastern Europe. Moreover, there are approximately
10,000 troops from the <color=#3366CC>United States Armed Forces</color> stationed across Poland. From 2024, Poland also provides
mandatory firearms training for pupils in <color=#3366CC>primary</color> and <color=#3366CC>secondary schools</color>.
Security, law enforcement and emergency services
Law enforcement in Poland is performed by several agencies which are subordinate to the Ministry of Interior and
Administration – the State Police (Policja), assigned to investigate crimes or transgression; the Municipal City Guard,
which maintains <color=#3366CC>public order</color>; and several specialised agencies, such as the Polish Border Guard. Municipal guards are
primarily headed by provincial, regional or city councils; individual guards are not permitted to carry <color=#3366CC>firearms</color> unless
instructed by the superior commanding officer. Security service personnel conduct regular patrols in both large urban
areas or smaller suburban localities.
Emergency services in Poland consist of the emergency medical services, <color=#3366CC>search and rescue</color> units of the Polish Armed
Forces and State Fire Service. Emergency medical services in Poland are operated by local and regional governments,
but are a part of the centralised national agency – the National Medical Emergency Service (Państwowe Ratownictwo
Medyczne). Thanks to its location, Poland is a country essentially free from the threat of natural disasters such as

<color=#3366CC>earthquakes</color>, volcanic eruptions, <color=#3366CC>tornadoes</color> and <color=#3366CC>tropical cyclones</color>. However, <color=#3366CC>floods</color> have occurred in low-lying areas
from time to time during periods of extreme rainfall, for example during the 2010 Central European floods.
The Internal Security Agency (ABW, or ISA in English) is the chief counterintelligence instrument safeguarding Poland's
internal security, along with Agencja Wywiadu (AW) which identifies threats and collects secret information abroad. The
Central Investigation Bureau of Police (CBŚP) and the Central Anticorruption Bureau (CBA) are responsible for
countering organised crime and corruption in state and private institutions.
Economy
Poland has a social market economy and is a regional economic power in East-Central Europe. As of 2025, the
country's gross domestic product (GDP) is the sixth largest in the European Union by <color=#3366CC>nominal standards</color>, the fifth
largest by purchasing power parity, and ranks 20th globally. It is one of the fastest growing within the Union and
reached a developed market status in 2018. The unemployment rate published by Eurostat in 2023 amounted to 2.8%,
which was the second-lowest in the EU. As of 2023, around 62% of the employed population works in the service
sector, 29% in manufacturing, and 8% in the agricultural sector, thus manifesting a highly diversified economy.
Although Poland is a member of the <color=#3366CC>European single market</color>, the country has not adopted the <color=#3366CC>Euro</color> as legal tender and
maintains its own currency – the Polish złoty (zł, PLN).
Poland is a regional European leader in terms of foreign direct investment and possesses around 40 percent of the 500
biggest companies in the region by revenues whilst maintaining a high globalisation rate and relatively high economic
competitiveness. The country's largest firms compose the WIG20 and WIG30 <color=#3366CC>stock market indexes</color>, which are traded
on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. The Central Statistical Office estimated that in 2014 there were 1,437 Polish
corporations with interests in 3,194 foreign entities. Poland also has the largest banking sector in East-Central Europe,
with 32.3 branches per 100,000 adults. The monetary policy is determined by the National Bank of Poland (NBP),
which controls the issuing of the national currency. It was the only European economy to have avoided the <color=#3366CC>recession of</color>
<color=#3366CC>2008</color>. Since 2019, workers under the age of 26 are exempt from paying the <color=#3366CC>income tax</color>.
The country is the 19th largest exporter of goods and services in the world. Exports of goods and services are valued at
approximately 58% of GDP, as of 2023. Poland's largest trade partners are Germany, the United Kingdom, the <color=#3366CC>Czech</color>
<color=#3366CC>Republic</color>, France, Italy, the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>. Among its lead exports are motor cars, buses, and
vehicle-related accessories, machinery, <color=#3366CC>electronics</color>, <color=#3366CC>electric batteries</color>, <color=#3366CC>home appliances</color>, furniture, cosmetics, military

equipment, and <color=#3366CC>tobacco</color> as well as materials such as silver, <color=#3366CC>copper</color>, <color=#3366CC>steel</color>, coal, <color=#3366CC>zinc</color>, <color=#3366CC>tar</color>, and <color=#3366CC>coke</color>. In 2023, the country
produced 1300 tonnes of silver and was the 5th largest silver producer globally. As of May 2026, Poland holds the
world's 11th largest gold reserve, estimated at 582 tonnes.
Tourism
In 2020, the total value of the <color=#3366CC>tourism industry</color> in Poland was 104.3 billion PLN, then equivalent to 4.5% of the Polish
GDP. Tourism contributes considerably to the overall economy and makes up a relatively large proportion of the
country's service market. Nearly 200,000 people were employed in the accommodation and catering (hospitality) sector
in 2020. In 2021, Poland ranked 12th most visited country in the world by international arrivals.
Tourist attractions in Poland range from the mountains in the south to the beaches on the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color> in the north. Many
trail of rich architectural and cultural heritage. Among the most recognisable landmarks are Old Towns in Kraków,
Warsaw, <color=#3366CC>Wrocław</color> (dwarf statues), <color=#3366CC>Gdańsk</color>, <color=#3366CC>Poznań</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lublin</color>, Toruń and Zamość as well as museums, zoological
gardens, theme parks and the Wieliczka Salt Mine, with its labyrinthine tunnels, <color=#3366CC>underground lake</color> and chapels carved
by miners out of <color=#3366CC>rock salt</color> beneath the ground. There are over 100 castles in the country, largely within the <color=#3366CC>Lower</color>
<color=#3366CC>Silesian Voivodeship</color> (including the Piast Castles Trail), and also on the Trail of the Eagles' Nests; the largest castle in
the world by land area is situated in Malbork. The German <color=#3366CC>Auschwitz concentration camp</color> in Oświęcim, and the Skull
Chapel in Kudowa-Zdrój constitute dark tourism. Regarding nature based travel, notable sites include the Masurian
Lake District and <color=#3366CC>Białowieża Forest</color> in the east; on the south Karkonosze, the Table Mountains, the Pieniny and the
Tatra Mountains, where Rysy and the Eagle's Path trail are located. The Bieszczady Mountains lie in the extreme
south-east.
Transport
Transport in Poland is provided by means of rail, road, marine shipping and air travel. The country is part of EU's
<color=#3366CC>Schengen Area</color> and is an important transport hub due to its strategic geographical position in Central Europe. Some of
the longest European routes, including the E30 and E40, run through Poland. The country has a good network of
highways consisting of express roads and <color=#3366CC>motorways</color>. As of August 2023, Poland has the world's 21st-largest road
network, maintaining over 5000 km of highways in use. In larger cities, <color=#3366CC>public transport</color> is heavily utilised; Poland is one
of Europe's largest bus and tram manufacturers, and hosts one of the biggest tram and light rail transit systems.
In 2022, the nation had 19393 km of railway track, the third longest in the European Union after Germany and France.
Polish State Railways (PKP) is the dominant railway operator, with certain major voivodeships or urban areas
possessing their own <color=#3366CC>commuter</color> and regional rail. Poland has a number of international airports, the largest of which is
Warsaw Chopin Airport. It is the primary global hub for LOT Polish Airlines, the country's flag carrier.
Seaports exist all along Poland's Baltic coast, with most freight operations using Świnoujście, Police, Szczecin,
Kołobrzeg, Gdynia, Gdańsk and Elbląg as their base. The Port of Gdańsk is the only port in the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color> adapted to
receive oceanic vessels. Polferries and Unity Line are the largest Polish ferry operators, with the latter providing
roll-on/roll-off and train ferry services to <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color>.
Energy
The electricity generation sector in Poland is largely <color=#3366CC>fossil-fuel</color>–based. Coal production in Poland is a major source of
employment and the largest source of the nation's <color=#3366CC>greenhouse gas emissions</color>. Many power plants nationwide use
Poland's position as a major European exporter of coal to their advantage by continuing to use coal as the primary raw
material in the production of their energy. The three largest Polish coal mining firms (Węglokoks, Kompania Węglowa
and JSW) extract around 100 million tonnes of coal annually. After coal, Polish energy supply relies significantly on
<color=#3366CC>natural gas</color> and oil.
The new Energy Policy of Poland until 2040 (EPP2040) would reduce the share of coal and lignite in electricity
generation by 25% from 2017 to 2030. The plan involves deploying new nuclear plants, increasing energy efficiency,
and decarbonising the Polish transport system in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and prioritise long-term
energy security. In March 2026, PEJ submitted an application for a permit to build a nuclear power plant.
Science and technology
Over the course of history, the Polish people have made considerable contributions in the fields of science, technology
and mathematics. Perhaps the most renowned Pole to support this theory was <color=#3366CC>Nicolaus Copernicus</color>, who triggered the
Copernican Revolution by placing the <color=#3366CC>Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the universe</color>. He also derived a
quantity theory of money, which made him a pioneer of economics. Copernicus' achievements and discoveries are
considered the basis of Polish culture and cultural identity. Poland was ranked 39th in the Global Innovation Index in
Poland's tertiary education institutions; traditional universities, as well as technical, medical, and economic institutions,
employ around tens of thousands of researchers and staff members. There are hundreds of research and development
institutes. However, in the 19th and 20th centuries many Polish scientists worked abroad; one of the most important of
these exiles was <color=#3366CC>Maria Skłodowska-Curie</color>, a physicist and chemist who lived much of her life in France. In 1925, she
established Poland's Radium Institute.
In the first half of the 20th century, Poland was a flourishing centre of mathematics. Outstanding Polish mathematicians
formed the Lwów School of Mathematics (with <color=#3366CC>Stefan Banach</color>, Stanisław Mazur, Hugo Steinhaus, <color=#3366CC>Stanisław Ulam</color>) and
Warsaw School of Mathematics (with <color=#3366CC>Alfred Tarski</color>, Kazimierz Kuratowski, <color=#3366CC>Wacław Sierpiński</color> and Antoni Zygmund).
Numerous mathematicians, scientists, chemists or economists emigrated due to historic vicissitudes, among them

<color=#3366CC>Benoit Mandelbrot</color>, <color=#3366CC>Leonid Hurwicz</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alfred Tarski</color>, Joseph Rotblat and Nobel Prize laureates Roald Hoffmann, <color=#3366CC>Georges</color>
<color=#3366CC>Charpak</color> and Tadeusz Reichstein.
Demographics
Poland has a population of approximately 38.2 million as of 2021, and is the ninth-most populous country in Europe, as
well as the fifth-most populous member state of the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>. It has a population density of 122 /km2. The total
fertility rate was estimated at 1.2 children born to a woman in 2023, which is among the world's lowest. Furthermore,
Poland's population is aging significantly, and the country has a median age of 42.2.
Around 60% of the country's population lives in urban areas or major cities and 40% in rural zones. In 2020, 50.2% of
Poles resided in <color=#3366CC>detached dwellings</color> and 44.3% in apartments. The most populous administrative province or state is
the <color=#3366CC>Masovian Voivodeship</color> and the most populous city is the capital, <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color>, at 1.8 million inhabitants with a further
2–3 million people living in its metropolitan area. The metropolitan area of <color=#3366CC>Katowice</color> is the largest urban <color=#3366CC>conurbation</color>
with a population between 2.7 million and 5.3 million residents. Population density is higher in the south of Poland and
mostly concentrated in Upper Silesia, between the cities of <color=#3366CC>Wrocław</color> and <color=#3366CC>Kraków</color>.
In the 2011 Polish census, 37,310,341 people reported Polish identity, 846,719 Silesian, 232,547 Kashubian and
147,814 German. Other identities were reported by 163,363 people (0.41%) and 521,470 people (1.35%) did not
specify any nationality. Official population statistics do not include migrant workers who do not possess a permanent
residency permit or Karta Polaka. More than 1.7 million Ukrainian citizens worked legally in Poland in 2017. The
number of migrants is rising steadily; the country approved 504,172 work permits for foreigners in 2021 alone.
According to the 2021 census, ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population, including people who declared Polish
heritage alone (96.28%) or both Polish and another ethnicity (2.56%) as responders were allowed to select up to two
ethnicities. People who declared only non-Polish ethnicities made up 1.13% of the population and people who did not
report their ethnicity numbered 0.03%. The province with the highest percentage of ethnic Poles was the <color=#3366CC>Holy Cross</color>
<color=#3366CC>Voivodeship</color> (99.70%), and the region with the lowest share of ethnic Poles was the <color=#3366CC>Silesian Voivodeship</color> (95.49%).
Languages
<color=#3366CC>Polish</color> is the official and predominant spoken language in Poland, and is one of the official languages of the European
Union. It is also a <color=#3366CC>second language</color> in parts of neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color>, where it is taught in Polish-minority schools.
Contemporary Poland is a linguistically homogeneous nation, with 97% of respondents declaring Polish as their mother
tongue. There are currently 15 minority languages in Poland, including one recognised regional language, Kashubian,
which is spoken by approximately 100,000 people on a daily basis in the northern regions of Kashubia and <color=#3366CC>Pomerania</color>.
Poland also recognises secondary administrative languages or auxiliary languages in bilingual municipalities, where
bilingual signs and placenames are commonplace. According to the Centre for Public Opinion Research, around 32%
of Polish citizens declared knowledge of the English language in 2015.
Religion
According to the 2021 census, 71.3% of all Polish citizens adhere to the Catholic Church, with 6.9% identifying as
having no religion and 20.6% refusing to answer.
Poland is one of the most religious countries in Europe, where Catholicism remains a part of national identity and
Polish-born <color=#3366CC>Pope John Paul II</color> is widely revered. In 2015, 61.6% of respondents outlined that religion is of high or very
high importance. However, church attendance has greatly decreased in recent years; only 28% of Catholics attended
mass weekly in 2021, down from around half in 2000. According to <color=#3366CC>The Wall Street Journal</color>, "Of [the] more than 100
countries studied by the Pew Research Center in 2018, Poland was <color=#3366CC>secularising</color> the fastest, as measured by the
disparity between the religiosity of young people and their elders."
Freedom of religion in Poland is guaranteed by the Constitution, and Poland's concordat with the <color=#3366CC>Holy See</color> enables the
teaching of religion in public schools. Historically, the Polish state maintained a high degree of religious tolerance and
provided asylum for refugees fleeing religious persecution in other parts of Europe. Poland hosted Europe's largest
Jewish diaspora, and the country was a centre of Ashkenazi Jewish culture and traditional learning until the <color=#3366CC>Holocaust</color>.
Contemporary religious minorities include Eastern Orthodox Church, <color=#3366CC>Protestants</color>, including <color=#3366CC>Lutherans</color> of the
Evangelical-Augsburg Church, <color=#3366CC>Pentecostals</color> in the Pentecostal Church in Poland, Adventists in the <color=#3366CC>Seventh-day</color>
<color=#3366CC>Adventist Church</color>. Other smaller Christian denominations include <color=#3366CC>Eastern Catholics</color>, Mariavites, <color=#3366CC>Evangelicalism</color>
denominations. Other religions include <color=#3366CC>Jehovah's Witnesses</color>, Jews, Muslims (<color=#3366CC>Tatars</color>), and <color=#3366CC>neopagans</color>, some of whom
are members of the Native Polish Church.
Health
Medical service providers and <color=#3366CC>hospitals</color> in Poland are subordinate to the Ministry of Health; it provides administrative
oversight and scrutiny of general medical practice and is obliged to maintain a high standard of <color=#3366CC>hygiene</color> and patient
care. Poland has a <color=#3366CC>universal healthcare system</color> based on an all-inclusive <color=#3366CC>insurance system</color>; state subsidised
healthcare is available to all citizens covered by the general health insurance programme of the National Health Fund
(NFZ). Private medical complexes exist nationwide; over 50% of the population uses both public and private sectors.
According to the <color=#3366CC>Human Development Report</color> from 2020, the average life expectancy at birth is 79 years (around 75
years for an infant male and 83 years for an infant female); the country has a low <color=#3366CC>infant mortality rate</color> (4 per 1,000
births). In 2019, Poland was the 15th-largest importer of <color=#3366CC>medications</color> and pharmaceutical products. In the same year,
the principal cause of death was <color=#3366CC>ischemic heart disease</color>; diseases of the <color=#3366CC>circulatory system</color> accounted for 45% of all
deaths. Moreover, the increasing rate of childhood <color=#3366CC>obesity</color> in Poland is one of the fastest in Europe. Health
professionals warn that if these rapid upward trajectories continue, the current generation of children could be the first
in modern history to have a shorter life expectancy than their parents due to obesity-related complications like <color=#3366CC>type 2</color>
<color=#3366CC>diabetes</color> and <color=#3366CC>hypertension</color>.
Education
The <color=#3366CC>Jagiellonian University</color> founded in 1364 by <color=#3366CC>Casimir III</color> in <color=#3366CC>Kraków</color> was the first institution of higher learning
established in Poland, and is one of the oldest universities still in continuous operation. Poland's Commission of
National Education (Komisja Edukacji Narodowej), established in 1773, was the world's first state ministry of education.
In 2018, the <color=#3366CC>Programme for International Student Assessment</color>, coordinated by the <color=#3366CC>Organisation for Economic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Co-operation and Development</color>, placed Poland's educational output as one of the highest in the OECD, ranking 5th by
student attainment and 6th by student performance in 2022.
The framework for primary, secondary and higher tertiary education are established by the Ministry of Education and
Science. One year of kindergarten is <color=#3366CC>compulsory</color> for six-year-olds. Primary education traditionally begins at the age of
seven, although children aged six can attend at the request of their parents or guardians. Elementary school spans
eight grades and secondary schooling is dependent on student preference – a four-year high school (liceum), a
five-year technical school (technikum) or various <color=#3366CC>vocational studies</color> (szkoła branżowa) can be pursued by individual
pupils. A liceum or technikum is concluded with a maturity exit exam (matura), which must be passed in order to apply
for a university or other institutions of higher learning.
In Poland, there are over 500 university-level institutions, with numerous faculties. The University of Warsaw and
Warsaw Polytechnic, the University of Wrocław, Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań and the University of
Technology in Gdańsk are among the most prominent. There are three conventional <color=#3366CC>academic degrees</color> in Poland –
<color=#3366CC>licencjat</color> or <color=#3366CC>inżynier</color> (first cycle), magister (second cycle) and <color=#3366CC>doktor</color> (third cycle qualification).
Culture
The culture of Poland is closely connected with its intricate 1,000-year <color=#3366CC>history</color>, and forms an important constituent in the
<color=#3366CC>Western civilisation</color>. The Poles take great pride in their national identity which is often associated with the colours white
and red, and exuded by the expression biało-czerwoni ("whitereds"). National symbols, chiefly the crowned white-tailed
eagle, are often visible on clothing, insignia and emblems. The architectural monuments of great importance are
protected by the National Heritage Board of Poland. Over 100 of the country's most significant tangible wonders were
enlisted onto the Historic Monuments Register, with further 18 being recognised by <color=#3366CC>UNESCO</color> as World Heritage Sites.
Holidays and traditions
There are 14 government-approved annual public holidays – New Year on 1 January, <color=#3366CC>Three Kings' Day</color> on 6 January,
<color=#3366CC>Easter Sunday</color> and Easter Monday, <color=#3366CC>Labour Day</color> on 1 May, Constitution Day on 3 May, <color=#3366CC>Pentecost</color>, Corpus Christi,
Feast of the Assumption on 15 August, All Saints' Day on 1 November, Independence Day on 11 November and
Christmastide on 24, 25 and 26 December.
Particular traditions and superstitious customs observed in Poland are not found elsewhere in Europe. Though
Christmas Eve (Wigilia) had not been a public holiday until 2025, it remains the most memorable day of the entire year.
<color=#3366CC>Trees</color> are decorated on 24 December, hay is placed under the tablecloth to resemble Jesus' manger, Christmas wafers
(opłatek) are shared between gathered guests and a twelve-dish meatless supper is served that same evening when
the first star appears. An empty plate and seat are symbolically left at the table for an unexpected guest. On occasion,
<color=#3366CC>carolers</color> journey around smaller towns with a folk Turoń creature until the <color=#3366CC>Lent</color> period.
A widely popular doughnut and sweet pastry feast occurs on Fat Thursday, usually 52 days prior to Easter. <color=#3366CC>Eggs</color> for
<color=#3366CC>Holy Sunday</color> are painted and placed in decorated baskets that are previously blessed by clergymen in churches on
Easter Saturday. Easter Monday is celebrated with pagan dyngus festivities, where the youth is engaged in water
fights. Cemeteries and graves of the deceased are annually visited by family members on All Saints' Day; tombstones
are cleaned as a sign of respect and candles are lit to honour the dead on an unprecedented scale.
Music and dance
Polish <color=#3366CC>classical music</color> encompasses medieval and early-modern liturgical tradition, regional <color=#3366CC>folk tunes</color>, and a

world-renowned <color=#3366CC>piano</color> legacy. Among the leading classical artists were <color=#3366CC>Frédéric Chopin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Artur Rubinstein</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ignacy Jan</color>

<color=#3366CC>Paderewski</color>, <color=#3366CC>Krzysztof Penderecki</color>, <color=#3366CC>Henryk Wieniawski</color>, <color=#3366CC>Karol Szymanowski</color>, <color=#3366CC>Witold Lutosławski</color>, and Stanisław
Moniuszko. Poland maintains a lively and diverse music scene which recognises its own music and entertainment
genres, such as sung poetry and disco polo. <color=#3366CC>Jazz</color> and <color=#3366CC>metal</color> genres are also particularly popular, and the country has
become a major venue for large-scale music festivals, chief among which are the Pol'and'Rock Festival, Open'er
Festival, Opole Festival and Sopot Festival.
The origins of Polish music can be traced to 13th-century polyphonic compositions associated with the Notre Dame
School. The anthemic melodies of Bogurodzica and God Is Born may also date back to this period, however, the first
notable composer, Nicholas of Radom, lived in the 15th century. In the 16th century, Venceslaus Samotulinus and
Mikołaj Gomółka gained recognition, and Diomedes Cato, an Italian <color=#3366CC>lutenist</color> at the court of Sigismund III, imported
musical styles from <color=#3366CC>southern Europe</color>. At the end of the 18th century, Polish classical music evolved into national forms,
and Wojciech Bogusławski is credited for composing the first Polish national opera in 1794. Halka and The Haunted
Manor are canons of 19th-century Polish opera. The <color=#3366CC>interwar period</color> of 1918–1939 saw the rise of <color=#3366CC>jazz</color>, <color=#3366CC>foxtrot</color>, Polish
<color=#3366CC>tango</color> and a strong <color=#3366CC>cabaret</color> culture.
Polish choreography is a sophisticated ethnographic system comprising five national folk dances; the polonaise,
mazurka, krakowiak (cracovienne), kujawiak, and oberek as well as various types of <color=#3366CC>polkas</color>. These are performed in
national costumes for larger cultural events and accompanied by instruments such as the <color=#3366CC>fiddle</color>, <color=#3366CC>bass</color>, <color=#3366CC>clarinet</color> and
<color=#3366CC>accordion</color> across much of Poland, and by the highlander <color=#3366CC>bagpipes</color> in the southern mountainous areas. Since 2023, the
polonaise has been inscribed in the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List. Polish dances also spread across much
of the <color=#3366CC>Nordic countries</color> and developed into the polska family of music and dance.
Art
Art in Poland has invariably reflected <color=#3366CC>European</color> trends, with Polish painting pivoted on <color=#3366CC>folklore</color>, Catholic themes,
<color=#3366CC>historicism</color> and <color=#3366CC>realism</color>, but also on <color=#3366CC>Impressionism</color> and romanticism. An important art movement was Young Poland,
developed in the late 19th century for promoting <color=#3366CC>decadence</color>, symbolism and <color=#3366CC>Art Nouveau</color>. Since the 20th century
Polish documentary art and photography has enjoyed worldwide fame, especially the Polish School of Posters. One of
the most distinguished paintings in Poland is <color=#3366CC>Lady with an Ermine</color> (1490) by <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>.
Internationally renowned Polish artists include <color=#3366CC>Jan Matejko</color> (historicism), Jacek Malczewski (symbolism), Stanisław
Wyspiański (art nouveau), Henryk Siemiradzki (Roman <color=#3366CC>academic art</color>), <color=#3366CC>Tamara de Lempicka</color> (<color=#3366CC>art deco</color>), and Zdzisław
Beksiński (dystopian <color=#3366CC>surrealism</color>). Several Polish artists and sculptors were also acclaimed representatives of
<color=#3366CC>avant-garde</color>, <color=#3366CC>constructivist</color>, <color=#3366CC>minimalist</color> and contemporary art movements, including Katarzyna Kobro, Władysław
Strzemiński, Magdalena Abakanowicz, Alina Szapocznikow, Igor Mitoraj and Wilhelm Sasnal.
Notable art academies in Poland include the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts, Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw, Art
Academy of Szczecin, University of Fine Arts in Poznań and the Geppert Academy of Fine Arts in Wrocław.
Contemporary works are exhibited at Zachęta, Ujazdów, and MOCAK art galleries.
Architecture
The architecture of Poland reflects <color=#3366CC>European architectural</color> styles, with strong historical influences derived from <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Low Countries</color>. Settlements founded on Magdeburg Law evolved around <color=#3366CC>central marketplaces</color> (plac,
rynek), encircled by a grid or concentric network of streets forming an old town (stare miasto). Poland's traditional
